title: How Fold Mountains Form

endcard.line: Footage: Dfromhimalayas (CC BY 4.0). Pictures: NASA (public domain); Kerk Phillips (public domain)

segments.say: What if the highest mountains on Earth began as mud at the bottom of a sea? The Himalayas did.

anim.title: Before the mountains
items: A sea, the Tethys, lies between
Rivers fill it with layers of mud and sand

segments.say: About two hundred million years ago, India began to drift north. Between it and Asia lay a sea, the Tethys, slowly filling with layers of sediment.
Squeeze soft layers from two sides and they bend, like a rug pushed against a wall. Geographers call that folding.
About forty to fifty million years ago, India ran into Asia. Both plates were too light to sink, so the crust between them crumpled upward.

numbers.sub: million years ago: India meets Asia

segments.say: The upfolds are called anticlines, and the downfolds are synclines. Together they make the long parallel ranges we see in the Himalayas.

anim.title: Still rising
items: Fossils of sea life in the rocks of Tibet

segments.say: The push has not stopped. The Himalayas still rise by more than a centimetre a year, and their rocks still carry fossils from that old sea.
For GS One: fold mountains are young, formed where plates converge, and the Himalayas are the textbook case.

sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 4 (Distribution of Oceans and Continents): India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago causing rapid uplift of the Himalayas; the process is still continuing
NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 5 (Geomorphic Processes): orogeny is mountain building through severe folding; upfolds are anticlines and downfolds synclines
NCERT Class 11, India: Physical Environment, ch. 2: the Himalayas are a series of parallel ranges with faults, folds and thrust planes

USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'The Himalayas: Two continents collide': Tethys Sea between India and Asia; India moved north after Pangaea broke up about 200 million years ago; similar rock density so neither plate subducted; Himalayas rise more than 1 cm a year; Tethys fossils in Tibetan sandstones

quiz.q: Why did the crust crumple upward when India met Asia?
options: One plate sank quickly under the other
Both plates were too light to sink, so the crust was pushed up
A volcano erupted under the sea
quiz.why: Both continental plates have about the same density, so neither sank and the crust rose.
Upfolds are anticlines; downfolds are synclines.

quiz.q: Roughly when did India collide with Asia?
quiz.why: NCERT and USGS both give about 40 to 50 million years ago.

reviewNote: Facts were read against NCERT Class 11 (Fundamentals of Physical Geography ch. 4 and 5; India: Physical Environment ch. 2) and the USGS 'This Dynamic Earth' page on the Himalayas. Diagrams are schematic, no map. The orbital photo is cropped to peaks; check that no place label shows. Moving facts: the uplift rate is an estimate and varies by study.
